verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Has Such a Thing Happened?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joel calls elders and people to hear and to tell the generations about a disaster without precedent (vv. 1-3). Wave after wave of locusts has eaten everything (v. 4). Drunkards weep because the wine is gone (v. 5), for a nation has come up against my land, powerful and beyond number (vv. 6-7). The land must lament like a young widow; offerings have ceased in the temple, and the fields, vines and trees are dried up, and gladness dries up from the children of man (vv. 8-12).
verseByVerse.theology: God speaks through disaster, and a people must stop and listen before life can go on as before.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD that came to Joel, the son of Pethuel: Hear this, you elders; give ear, all inhabitants of the land! Has such a thing happened in your days, or in the days of your fathers? Tell your children of it, and let your children tell their children, and their children to another generation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word of the LORD that came to Joel, the son of Pethuel:

We know almost nothing about Joel except his father's name. The verse gives no date and names no king. That is unusual, and it means we cannot be sure when Joel preached. Some believe he spoke early, perhaps in the ninth century BC. Many others think he spoke after the exile, when the temple had been rebuilt and Judah had no king. (The introduction explains both views.) But the important thing is stated plainly: this is the word of the LORD. What follows is not a farmer's report on crop damage. It is God speaking through a disaster.

Hear this, you elders; give ear, all inhabitants of the land! Has such a thing happened in your days, or in the days of your fathers?

Joel begins by calling everyone to attention, from the elders, the leaders and oldest members of the community, to all inhabitants of the land. And he asks a question that makes them search their memories: has anything like this ever happened? The oldest people in the land could not remember a disaster so great. When something unprecedented happens, God's people should ask what God is saying.

Tell your children of it, and let your children tell their children, and their children to another generation.

This disaster must be remembered and retold for four generations. Why? Because the lessons of God's dealings are meant to shape the future. Parents are to pass on not only happy stories of God's blessings but also sober stories of his judgments, so that children learn to fear the LORD. Every Christian family has stories of God's discipline and mercy that should be told at the dinner table.

verseByVerse.quote: What the cutting locust left, the swarming locust has eaten. What the swarming locust left, the hopping locust has eaten, and what the hopping locust left, the destroying locust has eaten. Awake, you drunkards, and weep, and wail, all you drinkers of wine, because of the sweet wine, for it is cut off from your mouth. For a nation has come up against my land, powerful and beyond number; its teeth are lions' teeth, and it has the fangs of a lioness. It has laid waste my vine and splintered my fig tree; it has stripped off their bark and thrown it down; their branches are made white.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What the cutting locust left, the swarming locust has eaten. What the swarming locust left, the hopping locust has eaten, and what the hopping locust left, the destroying locust has eaten.

Here is the disaster: locusts. For people in the West today, locusts may sound like a minor nuisance. In the ancient Near East they were one of the most terrifying catastrophes imaginable. A swarm could contain millions of insects, darken the sky, and strip every green leaf from the fields in a matter of hours. For a farming people, it meant famine.

Joel uses four names for the locusts: cutting, swarming, hopping and destroying. Some believe these describe the stages of a locust's growth, from young hopping insects to adults that fly. Others believe they describe wave after wave of swarms. Either way, the point is total devastation. Whatever one wave left, the next one ate. Nothing survived.

God had warned Israel that this could happen. Among the curses for breaking the covenant, Moses said, You shall carry much seed into the field and shall gather in little, for the locust shall consume it (Deut 28:38). The locusts were not random bad luck. They were a covenant warning.

Awake, you drunkards, and weep, and wail, all you drinkers of wine, because of the sweet wine, for it is cut off from your mouth.

The first people Joel addresses are the drunkards. They are the ones who would notice first, because the vineyards have been destroyed and there will be no more wine. There is a sharp point here. Some people only wake up to God when their pleasures are taken away. Awake, Joel says. Let this loss wake you up.

For a nation has come up against my land, powerful and beyond number; its teeth are lions' teeth, and it has the fangs of a lioness.

Joel describes the locust swarm as a nation, an invading army, powerful and beyond number. Their tiny teeth, multiplied by millions, were as destructive as a lion's. And notice the words my land. The land belonged to God. An attack on the land was an attack on what God had given his people.

It has laid waste my vine and splintered my fig tree; it has stripped off their bark and thrown it down; their branches are made white.

The vine and the fig tree were symbols of peace and prosperity in Israel (1 Kgs 4:25; Mic 4:4). The locusts had not only eaten the leaves and fruit but stripped the bark, leaving the branches bare and white like bones. It would take years for the trees to recover.

verseByVerse.quote: Lament like a virgin wearing sackcloth for the bridegroom of her youth. The grain offering and the drink offering are cut off from the house of the LORD. The priests mourn, the ministers of the LORD. The fields are destroyed, the ground mourns, because the grain is destroyed, the wine dries up, the oil languishes. Be ashamed, O tillers of the soil; wail, O vinedressers, for the wheat and the barley, because the harvest of the field has perished. The vine dries up; the fig tree languishes. Pomegranate, palm, and apple, all the trees of the field are dried up, and gladness dries up from the children of man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lament like a virgin wearing sackcloth for the bridegroom of her youth.

Joel calls the nation to grieve like a young bride whose husband has died just as their life together was beginning. (The ESV notes that virgin may be translated "young woman".) It is one of the most heartbreaking pictures of grief imaginable: everything she hoped for, gone in a moment. That is how deeply God's people should feel the loss, and what it means.

The grain offering and the drink offering are cut off from the house of the LORD. The priests mourn, the ministers of the LORD.

The worst result of the disaster was not economic but spiritual. Without grain and wine, the daily offerings in the temple could not be made. The worship of God itself was being disrupted. The priests mourned, not only because they were hungry, but because the fellowship between God and his people, expressed in those offerings, was being cut off.

The fields are destroyed, the ground mourns, because the grain is destroyed, the wine dries up, the oil languishes.

Be ashamed, O tillers of the soil; wail, O vinedressers, for the wheat and the barley, because the harvest of the field has perished.

The vine dries up; the fig tree languishes. Pomegranate, palm, and apple, all the trees of the field are dried up, and gladness dries up from the children of man.

The picture widens: grain, wine, oil, wheat, barley, vine, fig, pomegranate, palm and apple. The whole agricultural life of the nation had collapsed. The ESV notes that in Hebrew the words for dry up and be ashamed sound alike. As the land dries up, the people are put to shame. And the last phrase goes deepest: gladness dries up from the children of man. When God withdraws his blessings, joy itself withers.

Remember this in times of prosperity. Our joy often rests more than we realize on things God can remove in a day: health, income, food, comfort. The only joy that cannot dry up is joy in God himself. Habakkuk learned to say that even if the fig tree should not blossom, nor fruit be on the vines, yet I will rejoice in the LORD (Hab 3:17-18).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–20 — Cry Out to the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The priests must put on sackcloth, Consecrate a fast; call a solemn assembly, gather everyone to the house of the LORD, and cry out to the LORD (vv. 13-14). Alas for the day! For the day of the LORD is near (v. 15). Food and joy are cut off, seeds shrivel, cattle groan (vv. 16-18). The prophet prays: To you, O LORD, I call, for fire has devoured the land and even the beasts pant for God (vv. 19-20).
verseByVerse.theology: Present disasters are warnings of the great day of the LORD, and the right response is humble, united prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: Put on sackcloth and lament, O priests; wail, O ministers of the altar. Go in, pass the night in sackcloth, O ministers of my God! Because grain offering and drink offering are withheld from the house of your God. Consecrate a fast; call a solemn assembly. Gather the elders and all the inhabitants of the land to the house of the LORD your God, and cry out to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Put on sackcloth and lament, O priests; wail, O ministers of the altar. Go in, pass the night in sackcloth, O ministers of my God! Because grain offering and drink offering are withheld from the house of your God.

Now Joel tells the leaders what to do, and it begins with the priests. They are to put on sackcloth, the rough cloth of mourning, and spend the whole night in it, praying and lamenting. The spiritual leaders must lead the people in repentance. They cannot call others to humble themselves while remaining comfortable.

Consecrate a fast; call a solemn assembly. Gather the elders and all the inhabitants of the land to the house of the LORD your God, and cry out to the LORD.

Here is God's answer to disaster: Consecrate a fast; call a solemn assembly. Set aside a day for fasting. Call everyone together. Bring them to the house of the LORD. And cry out to the LORD.

This is exactly what God had promised to hear. When Solomon dedicated the temple, he prayed that if there was locust or caterpillar and God's people prayed toward that house, God would hear in heaven your dwelling place and forgive (1 Kgs 8:37, 39). And God answered: if my people who are called by my name humble themselves, and pray and seek my face and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven and will forgive their sin and heal their land (2 Chr 7:14).

Notice that the response is corporate. Everyone gathers, from the elders to the whole population. Churches today still need times when God's people set aside their normal routines to fast, pray and seek God together, especially in times of crisis.

verseByVerse.quote: Alas for the day! For the day of the LORD is near, and as destruction from the Almighty it comes. Is not the food cut off before our eyes, joy and gladness from the house of our God?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Alas for the day! For the day of the LORD is near, and as destruction from the Almighty it comes.

Now we come to the great theme of Joel's book: the day of the LORD. This phrase runs through the prophets. It means a day when God steps into history in power, to judge sin and to save his people. Many Israelites looked forward to it, assuming it would mean judgment on their enemies. But the prophets warned that God's own people would face it too. Amos said, Woe to you who desire the day of the LORD! ... It is darkness, and not light (Amos 5:18).

Joel sees the locust plague as a sign that this day is near. The disaster was a preview, a small taste of a far greater judgment. The ESV notes that in Hebrew destruction sounds like the Almighty. Destruction is coming from the Almighty. Isaiah used the very same words: Wail, for the day of the LORD is near; as destruction from the Almighty it will come! (Isa 13:6).

The New Testament tells us that the day of the LORD is still coming. The day of the Lord will come like a thief (1 Thess 5:2). And it tells us how anyone can face it. When Jesus hung on the cross, from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land (Matt 27:45). The darkness of the day of the LORD fell on him. He bore God's judgment so that those who trust in him can face the last day without fear.

Is not the food cut off before our eyes, joy and gladness from the house of our God?

The people could see it with their own eyes: no food, and no joy in the temple. The worship festivals, which were meant to be times of celebration, had become silent.

verseByVerse.quote: The seed shrivels under the clods; the storehouses are desolate; the granaries are torn down because the grain has dried up. How the beasts groan! The herds of cattle are perplexed because there is no pasture for them; even the flocks of sheep suffer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seed shrivels under the clods; the storehouses are desolate; the granaries are torn down because the grain has dried up.

Even the future was threatened. The locusts were followed by drought, and the seed planted for next year's crop shriveled in the dry ground. The storehouses were empty and falling apart. (The ESV notes that the meaning of the first line in Hebrew is uncertain, but the overall picture is clear.)

How the beasts groan! The herds of cattle are perplexed because there is no pasture for them; even the flocks of sheep suffer.

The animals suffer too. The cattle wander about perplexed, searching for grass that is not there. (The ESV notes that suffer may be "are made desolate".) Human sin affects all creation. Paul says that the whole creation has been groaning together (Rom 8:22), waiting for its redemption.

verseByVerse.quote: To you, O LORD, I call. For fire has devoured the pastures of the wilderness, and flame has burned all the trees of the field. Even the beasts of the field pant for you because the water brooks are dried up, and fire has devoured the pastures of the wilderness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To you, O LORD, I call. For fire has devoured the pastures of the wilderness, and flame has burned all the trees of the field.

Having called the people to pray, Joel now prays himself. To you, O LORD, I call. He does not only preach about prayer. He prays. And his prayer is honest. He describes exactly what he sees: drought so severe that it is like a fire burning up the pastures and trees.

This is what lament looks like in the Bible. It is not a complaint thrown at God from a distance, and it is not a cheerful pretense that everything is fine. It is bringing our pain honestly to God, because we believe he is the only one who can help.

Even the beasts of the field pant for you because the water brooks are dried up, and fire has devoured the pastures of the wilderness.

A striking picture ends the chapter: Even the beasts of the field pant for you. The thirsty animals, searching for water in dried-up streams, seem to cry out to God. If even the animals look to God, how much more should his people? The psalmist said, As a deer pants for flowing streams, so pants my soul for you, O God (Ps 42:1).

Chapter 1 leaves us in the middle of devastation, with no answer yet. But it shows us where to turn. When disaster comes, God's people do not first ask how to fix it. They gather, humble themselves, fast and cry out to the LORD. And they remember that every disaster in this world points to a greater day, a day that can only be faced safely in Christ, who thirsted on the cross so that we might drink from springs of living water (Rev 7:17).

1.title: Alas for the Day
1.overview:
The word of the LORD comes to Joel son of Pethuel. He calls the elders and all the people to consider whether such a thing has ever happened, and to tell it to their children for generations. Swarm after swarm of locusts has eaten everything. Drunkards are to weep because the wine is cut off, for a powerful, countless nation with lions' teeth has laid waste God's vine and fig tree (vv. 1-7).

The land is to lament like a young woman mourning the husband of her youth. Grain and drink offerings are cut off from the temple, and the priests mourn. The fields, grain, wine and oil are destroyed; the farmers and vinedressers are to wail, for all the trees are dried up and gladness has dried up (vv. 8-12).

The priests are to put on sackcloth and lament through the night. They must consecrate a fast, call a solemn assembly, gather the elders and all the people to the house of the LORD and cry out to him. The day of the LORD is near, coming as destruction from the Almighty. Food and joy are cut off, seed shrivels, storehouses are empty, and the cattle and sheep suffer (vv. 13-18).

Joel cries out to the LORD, for fire has devoured the pastures and trees, and even the wild animals pant for God because the brooks have dried up (vv. 19-20).
1.theology:
God speaks through disasters, which can be covenant warnings calling his people to attention (vv. 1-4; Deut 28:38).

God's dealings, including his judgments, are to be taught to the next generations (v. 3).

Joy that rests on God's gifts can dry up in a day; lasting joy is found in God himself (vv. 10-12; Hab 3:17-18).

The right response to disaster is humble, corporate repentance and prayer, led by spiritual leaders (vv. 13-14; 1 Kgs 8:37-39; 2 Chr 7:14).

Present judgments preview the great day of the LORD, which is still coming and which Christ bore for his people on the cross (v. 15; Isa 13:6; Amos 5:18; 1 Thess 5:2; Matt 27:45).

Sin affects the whole creation, which groans and looks to God (vv. 18-20; Rom 8:22; Ps 42:1).

Biblical lament brings honest pain to God in prayer (v. 19).
1.examples:
Old men searching their memories for anything like this.

Four waves of locusts, each eating what the last one left.

Drunkards told to wake up because the wine is gone.

Fig trees stripped white like bones.

A temple where the offerings have stopped.

A whole nation called to fast and pray together.

Thirsty cattle panting toward heaven.

The land is like the garden of Eden before them, but behind them a desolate wilderness, and nothing escapes them.<sup>4</sup>Their appearance is like the appearance of horses, and like war horses they run.<sup>5</sup>As with the rumbling of chariots, they leap on the tops of the mountains, like the crackling of a flame of fire devouring the stubble, like a powerful army drawn up for battle.<sup>6</sup>Before them peoples are in anguish; all faces grow pale.<sup>7</sup>Like warriors they charge; like soldiers they scale the wall. They march each on his way; they do not swerve from their paths.<sup>8</sup>They do not jostle one another; each marches in his path; they burst through the weapons and are not halted.<sup>9</sup>They leap upon the city, they run upon the walls, they climb up into the houses, they enter through the windows like a thief.<sup>10</sup>The earth quakes before them; the heavens tremble. Return to the LORD your God, for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love; and he relents over disaster.<sup>14</sup>Who knows whether he will not turn and relent, and leave a blessing behind him, a grain offering and a drink offering for the LORD your God?<sup>15</sup>Blow the trumpet in Zion; consecrate a fast; call a solemn assembly;<sup>16</sup>gather the people. Why should they say among the peoples, 'Where is their God?'"<sup>18</sup>Then the LORD became jealous for his land and had pity on his people.<sup>19</sup>The LORD answered and said to his people, "Behold, I am sending to you grain, wine, and oil, and you will be satisfied; and I will no more make you a reproach among the nations.<sup>20</sup>"I will remove the northerner far from you, and drive him into a parched and desolate land, his vanguard into the eastern sea, and his rear guard into the western sea; the stench and foul smell of him will rise, for he has done great things.<sup>21</sup>"Fear not, O land; be glad and rejoice, for the LORD has done great things!<sup>22</sup>Fear not, you beasts of the field, for the pastures of the wilderness are green; the tree bears its fruit; the fig tree and vine give their full yield.<sup>23</sup>"Be glad, O children of Zion, and rejoice in the LORD your God, for he has given the early rain for your vindication; he has poured down for you abundant rain, the early and the latter rain, as before.<sup>24</sup>"The threshing floors shall be full of grain; the vats shall overflow with wine and oil.<sup>25</sup>I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust has eaten, the hopper, the destroyer, and the cutter, my great army, which I sent among you.<sup>26</sup>"You shall eat in plenty and be satisfied, and praise the name of the LORD your God, who has dealt wondrously with you. verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Day of the LORD Is Great
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Blow a trumpet in Zion, for the day of the LORD is near, a day of darkness and gloom (vv. 1-2). A vast army comes, turning Eden into wilderness, running like war horses and scaling walls (vv. 3-9). Heaven and earth shake, and the LORD himself leads this army: For the day of the LORD is great and very awesome; who can endure it? (vv. 10-11).
verseByVerse.theology: The day of the LORD is overwhelming, and no one can endure it in his own strength.

verseByVerse.quote: Blow a trumpet in Zion; sound an alarm on my holy mountain! Let all the inhabitants of the land tremble, for the day of the LORD is coming; it is near, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and thick darkness! Like blackness there is spread upon the mountains a great and powerful people; their like has never been before, nor will be again after them through the years of all generations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blow a trumpet in Zion; sound an alarm on my holy mountain! Let all the inhabitants of the land tremble, for the day of the LORD is coming; it is near,

The trumpet here was a ram's horn, used to warn a city of attack. It is blown on my holy mountain, Zion, where the temple stood. The alarm is sounding in the very place of worship, and it is sounding because God himself is coming. The day of the LORD is coming; it is near.

a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and thick darkness! Like blackness there is spread upon the mountains a great and powerful people; their like has never been before, nor will be again after them through the years of all generations.

A dark cloud spreads across the mountains like the shadow of dawn in reverse. A locust swarm really can blot out the sun, and the plague of locusts in Egypt was described in similar terms: such a dense swarm of locusts as had never been before, nor ever will be again (Exod 10:14). Zephaniah used the same words for the day of the LORD: a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and thick darkness (Zeph 1:15).

Who is this great and powerful people? Christians have understood it in three main ways. Some believe Joel is describing the locusts of chapter 1 again, now pictured as an invading army. Others believe the locust plague was a warning of a real human army still to come, such as Assyria or Babylon, who would invade like locusts. Others see here a picture of the final day of judgment at the end of history. These are not entirely separate. Joel moves from the disaster in front of him to the greater judgments it points to. Every day of the LORD in history is a preview of the last one.

verseByVerse.quote: Fire devours before them, and behind them a flame burns. The land is like the garden of Eden before them, but behind them a desolate wilderness, and nothing escapes them. Their appearance is like the appearance of horses, and like war horses they run. As with the rumbling of chariots, they leap on the tops of the mountains, like the crackling of a flame of fire devouring the stubble, like a powerful army drawn up for battle.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fire devours before them, and behind them a flame burns. The land is like the garden of Eden before them, but behind them a desolate wilderness, and nothing escapes them.

The army turns paradise into desert. Before they arrive, the land is like the garden of Eden. After they pass, it is a desolate wilderness. It is a reversal of creation. Sin had already driven humanity out of Eden. Judgment strips away what remains of its beauty. (Later the prophets promise the opposite: God will make her wilderness like Eden, Isa 51:3.)

Their appearance is like the appearance of horses, and like war horses they run.

As with the rumbling of chariots, they leap on the tops of the mountains, like the crackling of a flame of fire devouring the stubble, like a powerful army drawn up for battle.

A locust's head does look like a small horse's head, and a swarm makes a roaring noise like chariots or a crackling fire. Revelation uses similar images for its demonic locusts: In appearance the locusts were like horses prepared for battle (Rev 9:7). Joel's description is vivid enough that his hearers could hear the roar.

verseByVerse.quote: Before them peoples are in anguish; all faces grow pale. Like warriors they charge; like soldiers they scale the wall. They march each on his way; they do not swerve from their paths. They do not jostle one another; each marches in his path; they burst through the weapons and are not halted. They leap upon the city, they run upon the walls, they climb up into the houses, they enter through the windows like a thief.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before them peoples are in anguish; all faces grow pale.

Like warriors they charge; like soldiers they scale the wall. They march each on his way; they do not swerve from their paths.

They do not jostle one another; each marches in his path; they burst through the weapons and are not halted.

This army is perfectly disciplined. No soldier breaks rank. No one bumps into the next. Weapons cannot stop them. Human defenses are useless against a judgment that God sends.

They leap upon the city, they run upon the walls, they climb up into the houses, they enter through the windows like a thief.

Nothing can keep them out: not city walls, not houses, not windows. They come in like a thief. That phrase is picked up in the New Testament: the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night (1 Thess 5:2). The day of the LORD does not wait for people to be ready. It breaks in.

verseByVerse.quote: The earth quakes before them; the heavens tremble. The sun and the moon are darkened, and the stars withdraw their shining. The LORD utters his voice before his army, for his camp is exceedingly great; he who executes his word is powerful. For the day of the LORD is great and very awesome; who can endure it?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The earth quakes before them; the heavens tremble. The sun and the moon are darkened, and the stars withdraw their shining.

Now the language grows cosmic. The whole creation shakes: earth, sky, sun, moon and stars. The prophets use this kind of language for the great interventions of God in history. And the New Testament uses it for the last day. Jesus said that after the tribulation the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light (Matt 24:29).

The LORD utters his voice before his army, for his camp is exceedingly great; he who executes his word is powerful. For the day of the LORD is great and very awesome; who can endure it?

Here is the shock. Whose army is this? It is his army. The LORD himself is at its head, shouting the commands. Israel's enemy, whether locust or soldier, is God's instrument. And the chapter's first section ends with a question that hangs in the air: who can endure it?

The honest answer is no one. No one can endure the day of the LORD in his own strength. Revelation asks the same question at the final judgment: the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand? (Rev 6:17). The only answer is the one God is about to give in the next verse.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Yet even now, says the LORD, return to me with all your heart, and rend your hearts and not your garments, for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love (vv. 12-14). The trumpet sounds again for a fast; everyone gathers, from elders to nursing infants, and the priests weep and pray, Spare your people, O LORD (vv. 15-17).
verseByVerse.theology: It is never too late to return to God, because his character is grace, and he calls for torn hearts, not religious show.

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet even now," declares the LORD, "return to me with all your heart, with fasting, with weeping, and with mourning; and rend your hearts and not your garments." Return to the LORD your God, for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love; and he relents over disaster.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Yet even now," declares the LORD, "return to me with all your heart, with fasting, with weeping, and with mourning;

After the terrifying description of judgment, three of the most hopeful words in the prophets: Yet even now. The army is coming, the day is near, but it is not too late. God himself speaks the invitation: return to me.

And he says how. With all your heart, not halfway. With fasting, with weeping, and with mourning, taking sin seriously. God does not want a casual "sorry". He wants repentance that feels the weight of what we have done.

and rend your hearts and not your garments." Return to the LORD your God, for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love; and he relents over disaster.

In Israel, people tore their clothes to show grief. But clothes can be torn without the heart ever changing. God says, rend your hearts and not your garments. Tear open your hearts before me. Outward religious signs mean nothing if the heart is untouched. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise (Ps 51:17).

And why should anyone dare to return? Because of who God is. For he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love. These are the words God used to describe himself to Moses at Mount Sinai (Exod 34:6), and they became Israel's great confession. Jonah quoted them too, complaining that God was too merciful to Nineveh (Jonah 4:2). God's character is the reason sinners can come back. He relents over disaster. He takes no pleasure in judgment and turns from it gladly when people repent.

verseByVerse.quote: Who knows whether he will not turn and relent, and leave a blessing behind him, a grain offering and a drink offering for the LORD your God?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who knows whether he will not turn and relent, and leave a blessing behind him, a grain offering and a drink offering for the LORD your God?

Who knows? Joel does not presume. Repentance is not a technique for forcing God's hand. But Joel hopes, because he knows God's character. And notice what he hopes for: that God would leave a blessing, enough grain and wine to restore a grain offering and a drink offering. The first thing he wants restored is not his own comfort but the worship of God. That is the mark of true repentance: longing not only for relief but for renewed fellowship with God.

verseByVerse.quote: Blow the trumpet in Zion; consecrate a fast; call a solemn assembly; gather the people. Consecrate the congregation; assemble the elders; gather the children, even nursing infants. Let the bridegroom leave his room, and the bride her chamber. Between the vestibule and the altar let the priests, the ministers of the LORD, weep and say, "Spare your people, O LORD, and make not your heritage a reproach, a byword among the nations. Why should they say among the peoples, 'Where is their God?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blow the trumpet in Zion; consecrate a fast; call a solemn assembly;

The trumpet blows again, but this time it is not an alarm of war. It is a summons to repentance. The same sound that announced judgment in verse 1 now calls people to prayer.

gather the people. Consecrate the congregation; assemble the elders; gather the children, even nursing infants. Let the bridegroom leave his room, and the bride her chamber.

No one is excused. The elderly, the children, even nursing babies are brought. Even a newly married couple on their wedding night, who under the law had special exemptions, must come. This was not a meeting for the especially devout. It was for everyone. When God's people face his judgment, the whole community stands before him together.

Between the vestibule and the altar let the priests, the ministers of the LORD, weep and say, "Spare your people, O LORD, and make not your heritage a reproach, a byword among the nations. Why should they say among the peoples, 'Where is their God?'"

The priests take their place between the vestibule and the altar, standing between the people and God, and they weep and pray. Their prayer is a model. They ask for mercy: Spare your people. They appeal to God's ownership: these are your people and your heritage. And they appeal to God's glory: if God's people are destroyed, the nations will mock, Where is their God? (The ESV notes that a byword may mean that the nations would rule over them.) The best prayers plead God's own name and honor.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–27 — I Will Restore the Years
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then the LORD became jealous for his land and had pity on his people (v. 18). He promises grain, wine and oil, removes the northern invader, and tells land, animals and people to rejoice, for the rains will come and the harvests overflow (vv. 19-24). I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust has eaten; they will eat, praise him and know that he is in their midst (vv. 25-27).
verseByVerse.theology: God answers repentance with pity, restoration and his own presence among his people.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD became jealous for his land and had pity on his people. The LORD answered and said to his people, "Behold, I am sending to you grain, wine, and oil, and you will be satisfied; and I will no more make you a reproach among the nations. "I will remove the northerner far from you, and drive him into a parched and desolate land, his vanguard into the eastern sea, and his rear guard into the western sea; the stench and foul smell of him will rise, for he has done great things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the LORD became jealous for his land and had pity on his people.

This verse is the turning point of the whole book. Everything before it is warning and lament. Everything after it is promise. God heard the prayers. He became jealous for his land, not jealous in a petty sense, but passionately protective, like a husband who will not let his bride be taken. And he had pity on his people.

The LORD answered and said to his people, "Behold, I am sending to you grain, wine, and oil, and you will be satisfied; and I will no more make you a reproach among the nations.

God answers their exact request. They prayed that they would not be a reproach, and he says, I will no more make you a reproach. They longed for grain and wine for the offerings, and he promises grain, wine, and oil, enough to be satisfied. God is not reluctant. When his people truly return, he answers with overflowing generosity.

"I will remove the northerner far from you, and drive him into a parched and desolate land, his vanguard into the eastern sea, and his rear guard into the western sea; the stench and foul smell of him will rise, for he has done great things.

God will drive the invader away. The eastern sea is the Dead Sea and the western sea the Mediterranean. (The ESV notes that vanguard is literally "face" and rear guard "his end".) Locust swarms have been known to die in the sea, rotting on the shore with a terrible smell. But Joel calls the invader the northerner, and locusts rarely came into Israel from the north. Many take this as a sign that Joel is speaking of a human army from the north, like Assyria or Babylon. Others think the locusts were driven by an unusual wind. Either way, God removes the threat completely. The one who has done great things in arrogance will be undone.

verseByVerse.quote: "Fear not, O land; be glad and rejoice, for the LORD has done great things! Fear not, you beasts of the field, for the pastures of the wilderness are green; the tree bears its fruit; the fig tree and vine give their full yield. "Be glad, O children of Zion, and rejoice in the LORD your God, for he has given the early rain for your vindication; he has poured down for you abundant rain, the early and the latter rain, as before. "The threshing floors shall be full of grain; the vats shall overflow with wine and oil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Fear not, O land; be glad and rejoice, for the LORD has done great things!

Now comes a beautiful reversal. The enemy has done great things (v. 20), but the LORD has done great things! The land that mourned in chapter 1 is told to rejoice.

Fear not, you beasts of the field, for the pastures of the wilderness are green; the tree bears its fruit; the fig tree and vine give their full yield.

The animals that groaned and panted for God (1:18, 20) are told, Fear not. The burned pastures turn green. The stripped fig tree and vine bear fruit again. Every picture of devastation in chapter 1 is answered with a picture of restoration.

"Be glad, O children of Zion, and rejoice in the LORD your God, for he has given the early rain for your vindication; he has poured down for you abundant rain, the early and the latter rain, as before.

Israel depended on two rainy seasons: the early rain in autumn to soften the ground for planting, and the latter rain in spring to bring the crops to maturity. God sends both. Notice that the people are to rejoice in the LORD your God, not just in the rain. The gift points to the Giver. And the phrase poured down prepares us for the greater pouring of verse 28.

"The threshing floors shall be full of grain; the vats shall overflow with wine and oil.

verseByVerse.quote: I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust has eaten, the hopper, the destroyer, and the cutter, my great army, which I sent among you. "You shall eat in plenty and be satisfied, and praise the name of the LORD your God, who has dealt wondrously with you. And my people shall never again be put to shame. You shall know that I am in the midst of Israel, and that I am the LORD your God and there is none else. And my people shall never again be put to shame.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust has eaten, the hopper, the destroyer, and the cutter, my great army, which I sent among you.

This is one of the most comforting promises in the prophets. I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust has eaten. (The ESV notes that restore may be translated "pay back".) The locusts had not only eaten one harvest. Their damage lasted years, because stripped trees and lost seed meant future harvests were lost too. God promises to make it up.

Notice also that God calls the locusts my great army, which I sent among you. God does not pretend the disaster came from somewhere else. He sent it as discipline. And the same God who sent it restores what it destroyed.

Many Christians have found comfort here for lost years in their own lives: years wasted in sin, lost to sickness, damaged by others or spent under God's discipline. We should be careful not to turn the verse into a promise that every earthly loss will be given back in this life. But the principle is true: the God who disciplines is also the God who restores, and in Christ nothing given to him is finally wasted. We know that for those who love God all things work together for good (Rom 8:28).

"You shall eat in plenty and be satisfied, and praise the name of the LORD your God, who has dealt wondrously with you. And my people shall never again be put to shame.

Restoration leads to worship. They eat, they are satisfied, and they praise the name of the LORD. The goal of God's blessings is always that we would know and praise him.

You shall know that I am in the midst of Israel, and that I am the LORD your God and there is none else. And my people shall never again be put to shame.

And here is the greatest gift of all: not grain and wine, but God himself. You shall know that I am in the midst of Israel. God's presence among his people is the heart of every blessing. The promise my people shall never again be put to shame is repeated twice for emphasis. Those who trust in God will not be disappointed.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh: sons and daughters, old and young, male and female servants (vv. 28-29). Wonders in heaven and earth will come before the great and awesome day of the LORD (vv. 30-31). And it shall come to pass that everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved, among the survivors whom the LORD calls (v. 32).
verseByVerse.theology: God promises to pour out his Spirit on all his people, and to save everyone who calls on his name, fulfilled from Pentecost onward in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions. Even on the male and female servants in those days I will pour out my Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions.

(The ESV notes that in the Hebrew Bible this verse begins chapter 3.)

Now the promise rises far above the harvest. Afterward, beyond the restoration of the land, God promises something new: I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh. In the Old Testament the Spirit came on particular people for particular tasks: prophets, judges, kings. Moses once wished that all the LORD's people were prophets, that the LORD would put his Spirit on them! (Num 11:29). Joel says that day is coming.

And notice who receives the Spirit. Your sons and your daughters: men and women alike. Your old men and your young men: every age. The Spirit will not be the privilege of a few religious professionals. He will be given to all God's people.

Even on the male and female servants in those days I will pour out my Spirit.

Even the lowest members of society, servants and slaves, will receive the Spirit. No one is too insignificant. Paul later rejoiced that in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body—Jews or Greeks, slaves or free—and all were made to drink of one Spirit (1 Cor 12:13).

This promise was fulfilled on the day of Pentecost. When the Holy Spirit came on the first Christians and they spoke in many languages, Peter stood up and said, this is what was uttered through the prophet Joel, and he quoted this very passage, beginning And in the last days it shall be, God declares, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh (Acts 2:16-17). And he explained who had poured out the Spirit: Jesus, Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you yourselves are seeing and hearing (Acts 2:33). The Spirit that Joel promised is the gift of the risen Christ.

Every Christian today has received this gift. Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (Rom 8:9). And all flesh reached even further than Peter expected, when the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles (Acts 10:45).

verseByVerse.quote: "And I will show wonders in the heavens and on the earth, blood and fire and columns of smoke. The sun shall be turned to darkness, and the moon to blood, before the great and awesome day of the LORD comes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And I will show wonders in the heavens and on the earth, blood and fire and columns of smoke.

The sun shall be turned to darkness, and the moon to blood, before the great and awesome day of the LORD comes.

The outpouring of the Spirit comes before the great and awesome day of the LORD, and signs in heaven and earth will announce that day: blood and fire and columns of smoke, a darkened sun and a blood-red moon.

How do these verses fit with Pentecost? Christians have answered in different ways. Many in the Reformed tradition believe that Pentecost began the last days, the whole age between Christ's first and second comings. On this view, some of these signs were already seen when there was darkness over the whole land while Jesus hung on the cross (Luke 23:44), and the full fulfillment will come at the final day, when Revelation says the sun became black as sackcloth, the full moon became like blood (Rev 6:12). Others, especially dispensationalists, believe Pentecost was a partial or preview fulfillment, and that a fuller outpouring of the Spirit on Israel, with the cosmic signs, awaits the end of history. Both agree that the Spirit has been poured out and that the great day is still coming.

The point for us is urgent. We live between the outpouring of the Spirit and the final day. This is the time to call on the Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: And it shall come to pass that everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved. For in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there shall be those who escape, as the LORD has said, and among the survivors shall be those whom the LORD calls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And it shall come to pass that everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved. For in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there shall be those who escape, as the LORD has said, and among the survivors shall be those whom the LORD calls.

Here is the answer to the question of verse 11: who can endure it? Everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved. Not everyone who is strong enough, good enough or religious enough. Everyone who calls. To call on the name of the LORD is to cry out to God in trust, depending on him alone for rescue.

Paul quotes this verse in Romans 10, and applies it directly to Jesus. He says, if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved, and then, For "everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved" (Rom 10:9, 13). The LORD of Joel is the Lord Jesus. To call on the name of Jesus is to call on the God of Israel. That is one of the clearest testimonies in the New Testament that Jesus is God.

And notice the everyone. Paul adds, For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek (Rom 10:12). The door of salvation is open to anyone, of any nation, background or past, who calls on the Lord.

The verse ends with a matching truth: among the survivors shall be those whom the LORD calls. We call on the Lord, and the Lord calls us. Peter joined these two ideas at Pentecost: the promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself (Acts 2:39). Our calling on him rests on his calling of us. Salvation is freely offered to all, and those who come find that God first drew them. That is grace from beginning to end.

2.title: I Will Pour Out My Spirit
2.overview:
The trumpet is to sound in Zion, for the day of the LORD is near, a day of darkness and gloom. A great and powerful people like no other spreads over the mountains, turning a land like Eden into wilderness. They look like horses, sound like chariots and fire, march in perfect order, scale walls and enter houses like a thief. Earth quakes, heavens tremble and the lights of heaven are darkened, for the LORD leads his army, and the great and awesome day of the LORD is one no one can endure (vv. 1-11).

Yet even now the LORD calls his people to return with all their heart, with fasting, weeping and mourning, rending their hearts and not their garments, for he is gracious, merciful, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love and relenting over disaster; who knows whether he will leave a blessing? The trumpet is to call a fast and gather everyone, from elders to infants, and the priests are to weep and pray that God spare his people from reproach among the nations (vv. 12-17).

Then the LORD becomes jealous for his land and pities his people. He promises grain, wine and oil, removes the northern invader, and calls the land, the animals and the children of Zion to rejoice, for he sends the early and latter rains and full harvests. He will restore the years the locusts ate; they will eat, praise him and know that he is in their midst, and they will never again be put to shame (vv. 18-27).

Afterward God will pour out his Spirit on all flesh, so that sons and daughters prophesy, old men dream and young men see visions, even servants. He will show wonders in heaven and earth before the great day of the LORD. Everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved, and in Zion there will be survivors whom the LORD calls (vv. 28-32).
2.theology:
The day of the LORD is overwhelming, God himself leads its army, and no one can endure it in his own strength (vv. 1-11; Zeph 1:15; Rev 6:17).

It is never too late to return to God, who calls for torn hearts rather than religious display (vv. 12-13; Ps 51:17).

God's character, gracious, merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, is the ground of hope for sinners (v. 13; Exod 34:6; Jonah 4:2).

True repentance involves the whole community and seeks God's glory and renewed worship, not only relief (vv. 14-17).

God answers repentance with pity, restoration and his own presence, and he can redeem lost years (vv. 18-27; Rom 8:28).

God promised to pour out his Spirit on all his people without distinction of sex, age or status, fulfilled at Pentecost by the exalted Christ (vv. 28-29; Acts 2:16-18, 33; 1 Cor 12:13; Rom 8:9).

Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord, who is Jesus, will be saved, and those who call are those whom God calls (v. 32; Rom 10:9-13; Acts 2:39).
2.examples:
An alarm trumpet blown in the temple courts.

A garden of Eden in front of the army and a wilderness behind it.

Locusts coming through the windows like thieves.

"Yet even now."

Torn hearts instead of torn clothes.

A bride and groom called from their wedding chamber to a prayer meeting.

Lost years restored.

The Spirit poured out on servants and grandmothers alike.
